utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-01-48-PT, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I have the appearances, please. For the Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May it please, Your Honours. Sureta Chana, Phil Weiner, Manoj Sachdeva, and David Re for the Prosecution, assisted by Ana Vrljic, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a question to you: In the latest filings from the Defence -- oh, I'm sorry, I got confused, you know, with all those documents, all the latest filings. Yeah. I'm sorry about that. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. May it please, the Court. My name is Peter Morrissey, I appear for Mr. Sefer Halilovic, and with me is Mr. Mettraux. And we are assisted by Mr. Amir Cengic, who's a legal assistant, and also present in court is Medina Delilac, investigator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I noted that the Defence also have an armada of the Defence counsels. This is very rare.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Halilovic, can you hear the proceedings in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I won't ask you the same question every day, but if you have any problems to follow the proceedings, please let me know as soon as possible. And I'll ask you some questions: When did you arrive in The Hague after your provisional release?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I arrived on Thursday evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. The Trial Chamber has noted that Mr. Halilovic arrived in -- in the UN Detention Unit on the 20th of January, 2005, after the provisional release. Do you have anything to complain at this stage?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Everything is in good order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready for trial?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. This is a Pre-Trial Conference held in accordance with Rule 73 bis (A) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal. Under a decision rendered by the Presiding Judge of the Trial Chamber on the 18th January 2005 to discuss some specific issues with the aim to prepare and facilitate the proceedings. By the order of the President, dated the 17th of January, 2005, the case is assigned to Trial Chamber I. The Bench will probably be composed of Judge El Mahdi, from Egypt, an ad litem Judge, Szenasi, from Hungary, and me, Judge Liu, from China. The party met by a written decision to this effect rendered by the President of the Tribunal tomorrow. Today we have a very heavy agenda. There are several issues to be discussed: Namely, the outstanding issues, outstanding motions, witness lists, exhibits, guidelines for the admission of the evidence, case presentation, and possibly any agreed facts, if there's any. Frankly speaking, I only got some materials of this case in less than a week's time, and I'm not quite familiar with the case at this moment, so this Pre-Trial Conference might be the first phase. If necessary, we will have the second phase of it on Thursday morning. Let us begin with the easiest one, that is, the case presentation. According to the schedule, this trial will commence on next Monday, the 31st of January, at 9.00 in the morning in Courtroom III with the opening statement of the Prosecution. Are there any questions on the side of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Philip Weiner for the Office of the Prosecutor. On Monday, the 31st at 12.00, two of the attorneys on this case have to take a judgement, the Strugar instrument. The senior trial attorney, Susan Somers, is in the United States, or will be leaving for the United States on Wednesday, and the two remaining senior counsel of the four counsel on that, both Mr. Re and myself, were planning to attend or we have to be there as the two lead counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think Monday morning we are only going to deal with the opening statement. Could you please tell me who is going to deliver that opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Attorney Sureta Chana. So if it's just the opening statements, then the -- the session should end by noontime and we could then attend the judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could I have any indication how long that opening statement will last? Just give me a rough idea. Wine --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: One and a half to two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That shouldn't be a problem, Your Honour. We should be available in the other courtroom at 12.00 then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And by the way, during the opening statement, we believe that no objection is allowed since this is just a presentation of the theory of the case by one side, which means this is the views expressed by one side. Unless there is some very serious mischaracterisation of the common facts, the other party may raise some comments or suggestions on that. Is that understandable?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we agree and we'll abide by that. We should make the comment that we understand exactly how Your Honour puts that. We are concerned that the opening statement remain within the pleadings. We will listen carefully, but we will not interrupt. Any comments we have to make, we shall make at the end of that opening speech, if that is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we will see at that time. The trial will commence on the five-day-a-week schedule. The Trial Chamber may adjust its schedule as necessary due to witness-related issues, specific requests by the parties, and unforeseen circumstances. Each day we'll have three sittings, and each sitting will last for about 80 minutes, with two breaks in between. Each will be 20 minutes, since we'll only have one witness -- one accused in this trial. The case will be heard in Courtroom III throughout the trial since this is the only courtroom with the e-court system, which is supposed to be a non-paper trial. Frankly speaking, it is also something new to the Judges in our whole judicial career. Fortunately, we have technicians ready to help us at any time of the proceedings. There's only two matters I would like to mention in this aspect: First, we should welcome the trial proceedings of twenty-first century with an open heart; secondly, I would like to remind both parties to present their case slowly and clearly. Some counsel may argue that might reduce the effect of the persuading force of their argument, but what is most important and effective way is to let the Judges and interpreters to understand your point and let the court reporter type down whatever you said in your statement. To facilitate the proceedings, the party calling the witness or presenting evidence through the witness shall provide a list of witnesses and documents to the court deputy one or two days before so that he could be very prepared to find out the documents which are going to be used in the hearings. At this moment, I would like to remind the parties that there are some amendments on the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal which might affect our case. For instance, the Rule 98 bis on the judgement of acquittal has been amended by the Plenary last December, which implies there might be a shorter interval between the Prosecution's case and the Defence case. At this moment, I would like to know whether the accused would like to make a statement in accordance with the Rule 84 bis after the Prosecutor's opening statement. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answer to that inquiry is no, he does not wish to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But I have to remind you that from the Rule of the Procedure understand that the accused has the right to make a statement at any time during the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions, any issues concerning with the ways of presenting the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is one question arising from Your Honour's ruling a moment ago about the provision of -- or list of witnesses and documents to the court deputy one to two days before the witness is called to give evidence. Our query is: Does that relate to cross-examination as well? We are aware that in different Trial Chambers different practices occur, both in the more common-law type Chambers and the more civil-law benches. We seek Your Honour's guidance in relation to the provision of notice to the other side as to whether or not we have to inform the other side as to which documents we intend to use in cross-examination of witnesses. The Prosecution submits that what is good for one side must be good for the other, whatever Your Honour's ruling is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey, do you have any comments on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, if Your Honour seeks submissions at this stage, our submission is that it shouldn't be required at this stage. There is some merit in what my learned friend says about equality between the parties in the practices, and I would respectfully agree. But our submission is that unless there's a pressing reason to do so in the circumstances of a case, and it's conceded that there are some cases where that may be needed, then the normal course is that it shouldn't be required, that the documents to be put or potentially to be put during a cross-examination have to be disclosed in advance. Often we don't know if we're going to be putting such documents until a particular line of answers may occur. For those reasons, unless there be a good reason to depart from that, I would submit there's no need for us to do so, nor at this stage can I see a pressing argument for the Prosecution to be compelled in a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the purpose of this ruling is to let the court deputy be prepared and to facilitate the proceedings of the case. So there's a strict requirement from the parties having their case in chief. As for the parties for the cross-examination, we are looking for your bona fide attitude in this aspect. There's no strict requirement for the parties cross-examining the witness to present that list beforehand. I understand that during the direct examination there might be some questions raised which requires some new materials to be presented in the cross-examination of that witness. That is quite natural and reasonable. But I still hope that the parties could inform the court deputy beforehand or maybe even before they start their cross-examining that witness on the materials they are going to use because in this case we are going to have the first taste of the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, we hear and accept what Your Honour says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. The next issue is about the guideline of the admission of evidence. There are some guidelines in the admission of the evidence in this case. I will mention some elements in this guideline. If it's required, the party could issue it in a written form. First, the parties should always bear in mind the basic distinction that exists between the admissibility of documentary evidence and the weight that documentary evidence is given under the principle of a free evaluation of evidence. The practice will be, therefore, in favour of admissibility as the rule. Secondly, the fact that this Trial Chamber may rule on admissibility of some particular document or other piece of evidence will not prevent the ruling being reversed. In the case of non-admission, at a later stage, as further evidence emerges that is relevant, has probative value and hence justified admission of the evidence in question. In a case of the admission into the evidence, a decision may be quashed if good cause is shown for doing so. Thirdly, the mere admission of documents into evidence does not in itself signify that statements contained therein will necessarily be deemed to be an accurate portrayal of the facts. Factors such as authenticity and proof of authorship will naturally assume greatest importance in the Trial Chamber's assessment of the weight to be attached to individual pieces of evidence. Fourthly, when objections are raised on the grounds of authenticity or reliability, this Trial Chamber will follow the practice this Tribunal has previously adopted; namely, to admit documents and video recordings, then decide what weight to give them in the context of the trial record as a whole. On request of a party or proprio motu the Bench may order the party tendering copies of the evidence to present the original or the best legible, audible, visible copy available. Fifth, there's no blanket prohibition on admission of documents. Simply on the grounds that the purported author has not been called to testify. Simply the fact that a document is unsigned or unstamped does not, a priori, render it void of authenticity. Authenticity and proof of authorship will assume the greatest importance in the Trial Chamber's assessment of the weight to be attached to individual pieces in the framework of the free evaluation of evidence. Sixth, hearsay evidence here is admissible out of court statements which a Trial Chamber considers probative admissible under Rule 89(C), as it was stated by the Appeals Chamber in Aleksovski case. The Trial Chamber has a broad discretion under Rule 89(C) to admit relevant hearsay evidence. Seventh, the best-evidence rule will be applied in the determination of matters before this Trial Chamber. This essentially means the Trial Chamber will rely on the best evidence available in the circumstances of the case and the parties are directed to regulate the production of their evidence along these lines. What is the best evidence will of course depend on the particular circumstances attached to each document and to the complexity of this case and the investigations that preceded it. Eighth, Rule 95 provides for the exclusion of improperly obtained evidence. It declares that no evidence shall be admissible if obtained by methods that cast substantial doubts on its reliability or if this admission is antithetical; two, and would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings. Ninth, the Trial Chamber emphasises what it considers to be the overriding principle in the matters of admissibility of evidence. The Trial Chamber is pursuant to the Statute of the Tribunal, the guardian and the guarantor of the procedural and substantive right of the accused. In addition, it has the obligation to strike a balance in seeking to protect the rights of victims and witnesses. Finally, the Trial Chamber may be obliged to produce evidence proprio motu as foreseen in the Rules. Are there any questions from the parties concerning with those guidelines? Maybe we could have a more clear picture when you get the written guidelines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we -- there are a couple of matters that I would seek to respond to, Your Honour, and I could do so more briefly and focusedly if I could wait and get the written guidelines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one matter I will bring up in respect of exhibits that you've just outlined, and that would be that I know that the Defence has an obligation to indicate to the Chamber as to what exhibits they would be objecting to on the grounds of authenticity or any other way. And it would assist the smooth process of this trial if we could actually know that, because we have already filed an exhibit list before this Chamber, and we would like to introduce that into evidence as bulk, and given this e-court, perhaps it will facilitate it if all the exhibits are entered into evidence and if the Defence would like to object to any particular exhibits, then they can indicate those. Otherwise, we could introduce our exhibits in a bulk form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There are a lot of filings from the Defence team, but I did not find any response to the Prosecution's motions concerning the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I'm -- well, we can respond to that by saying that there has been an extremely recent response filed in relation to that, which if it has not reached Your Honour now will do so this afternoon but is now filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much indeed. Now let's come to the outstanding motions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I -- would Your Honour excuse me a moment, please. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: May I respond to the matter raise by my learned friend, Ms. Chana, a moment ago very briefly without entering into a debate and argument about it at this stage. Your Honour, we are now in a position to give an indication about the exhibit list yet for a number of reasons. The Prosecution exhibit list is not to be relitigated in this court because there are motions before you already, but it's safe to say and uncontroversial to say that that exhibit list is very volatile right now, and there are a number of reasons why the Defence must be very cautious in making the concessions that are sought. As you will see from the filings, there's been some concern about a particular investigator, and there has been ongoing concern about the -- the volatility of that list. We are keen to be cooperative, and we will be, but as I think the Prosecution would readily appreciate at this moment, we can't be. And therefore, I would ask that that question be deferred until the Chamber has ruled on the relevant motions which touch upon that very matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe we could revisit this issue on Thursday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It seems to me that both parties agreed with this proposal. Now, let's come to the outstanding motions. Frankly speaking, I -- at this moment I don't know how many motions are pending at this moment because in the last two hours I received about four motions from the Defence team. Let me deal with them one by one. And if I miss something, I believe that the capable Defence team will remind me about that. The first one is filed on the 20th January, a motion for striking out paragraphs in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. Any response from the Prosecution side? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The response in brief, Your Honour, is that we received this document today. I first saw it about an hour and a half ago. We are not in any position today to orally -- orally respond to it in any detail. However, I can certainly foreshadow our response will be along the lines of the pre-trial brief as filed is not evidence. The Defence well and truly are on notice of the nature of our case from the statements we have disclosed to them. The exhibits on our exhibit list, the pre-trial brief, both versions, the notice we gave to the Defence in the purported supplement to the pre-trial brief, which although the Trial Chamber ruled against its admission -- against its filing as a supplement or amendment to the pre-trial brief, the Prosecution maintains it's still notice to the Defence as to the legal case theory. We do concede the last portion of the -- the last paragraph of the motion filed -- field today in relation to paragraph 207 and the accused's alleged responsibility as a deputy commander of the army. We concede - I'll say it straight up right now - that what is in the pre-trial brief is incorrect. That's at paragraph 39 of the motion. We concede that and we don't push that, don't seek for it to be relied upon. But our response is generally that the Defence are on proper notice of what our case is and we will respond to the details in that within the time over the next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think you are luckier than I am because I only got this document 30 minutes before the start of this trial. So I believe that, you know, we are not in the position to discuss it in details for this motion. But I shared the views expressed by the Prosecution. I feel very strange and awkward for a Defence team to file this kind of motion to strike some paragraphs, some words, from the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. As I said, that the pre-trial brief is just like an opening statement, which reflected the one-sided view of the party. I understand that the Defence team could not totally agree with the positions of the Prosecution. That's quite natural. But I don't think there's any necessity for the Defence to file a motion asking for the striking out certain paragraphs. But anyway, we will deal with it maybe on Thursday. Yes. The next motion is the motion for the postponement of witness testimony and for full disclosure of the relevant materials. I am not quite familiar with this motion. Maybe, Mr. Morrissey, you could brief me a little bit on this motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I can indicate to Your Honour why it is and the rationale for the motion. Is that what Your Honour seeks? Some guidance as to it? Your Honour, Salko Gusic is a witness currently proposed to be called by the Prosecutor. He's one of three witnesses who is at a higher level within the army command, and in particular -- he is in fact the commander or was the commander at the time of the 6th Corps in the -- in whose line of responsibility or, according to the Crown case near to whose -- the Prosecutor's case, near to whose assigned a responsibility this all took place. Now, in dealing with Mr. Gusic at an early stage, the Defence foresees -- or sees a number of problems. And I can list what they are and indicate why it is that we seek that he be called later and why it is that we seek to engage Your Honour in this discussion at all rather than simply doing it by discussion with the Prosecutor. First of all, we have very recently been provided with material indicating that Mr. Salko Gusic was in fact interviewed as a suspect himself. We are told with respect to -- and it is the case, with respect to other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Morrissey, I do -- don't know about the status of this witness, whether there are any protective measures. And the -- do we need to go to the private session? I'm seeking the advice from the Prosecution's case -- the Prosecution's team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I indicate I'm not aware of any, but the Prosecutor may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, although there are no measures at this time, if one is going to talk about allegations against the person, I think it should be in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But, Mr. Morrissey, I don't think that we should go into the very details of this motion at this stage. I just want to hear the kind of, you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- outline of your motion, you know. You may, you know, give us a very rough idea, though, about how this motion is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: If Your Honour is imposing the 30-second limit. I'll abide by that. The limit is that -- the areas of concern are, firstly, when a time to find out whether there's any more to know about Mr. Gusic; secondly, we think that he if were to be called early, he'd be a witness who lacks context. Being a higher-level witness, the Court being unaware of the crime base and of the reasons why his role is of some importance in the case, it would require an artificial examination-in-chief by the Prosecutor, assuming a lot of facts which haven't been proved yet, and it would impact on cross-examination as well because it would mean we'd have to cross-examine him about facts that he either knew or should have known or might have known without Your Honour having any idea of those facts, of their importance, of whether the Court's inclined to accept them or not. And in short, it would lead to a very artificial situation in dealing with this witness. It's not for the Defence to indicate why the -- what order the Prosecution should call witnesses, but it is for the Defence to indicate the difficulties it would cause us and the difficulties we think it might cause you, the Tribunal. We think if he was called early, you'd get an artificial view of him and we would find ourselves in some difficulties making the cross-examination mean something because the crime base and other matters from, if you like, lower-down witnesses were not yet established. So that there really are two matters: First of all, there may be developments about Mr. Gusic himself - we think there will be, but we certainly want time to check - and secondly, it would cause an artificiality and make it more difficult for the Court to properly assess what probative weight to give him and his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you did a pretty good job. Well, you know, I think we'll deal with this matter at a later stage. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I was going to respond now, since this witness is the third witness to be called at this point, or we can wait till Thursday, whatever Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I think the best way is for us to wait until Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm reminded -- I'm sorry to lengthen my 30 seconds. May I just mention this: There remains material concerning -- concerning Mr. Gusic which we await from the Prosecution, and we urgently want that to be provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no material. In fact, there is a misstatement in their motion. They've indicated that they had not received a transcript of the suspect interview, which we have a signed receipt of their -- of their receipt of their receiving that transcript. And that's on the 17th of January, 2005. Other than that, if you -- if the Court would like to wait till Thursday, there is no additional material in relation to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I hope that both parties could meet after this sitting and try to iron out any wrinkles on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will do so. However, let me indicate that when my friend, Mr. Weiner, points out to the Court that there's an error, he's also got a corrigendum provided to him by us indicating that. So that error was acknowledged sometime ago. However, Your Honour, we will iron out --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, excuse me. That's wrong. There were two motions filed in a row. In each one they claimed they had not received a transcript. With regard to the first witness, they have filed a notice of an error. They have not filed it with regard to the second motion they have filed. They made the same mistake again, and there has no -- no correction has been filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: There's no need to argue here at this moment. I have already ruled that after this sitting the parties should meet together to solve this problem. And we are expecting a report from the parties on Thursday morning. The next issue is about the videolink conference. Any objections from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The videolink conference, Your Honour, it relates to the witnesses Miletic and Pranjic. Your Honour, the evidence that's been provided to us at this stage renders us unable to consent to it. But I wanted to put this on the record that I've been given some advice orally about the situation for those two potential witnesses. And if that is confirmed in writing, we are going to consent. However, the current state of the materials is such that we cannot. Rather than engage the Court in that, you may permit us to iron out those wrinkles by Thursday and we -- they will be ironed out one way or other by that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Morrissey, I think this trial is supposed to be a non-paper trial, which means that you have to reduce the paperwork as much as possible. We try to solve all problems in the courtroom orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I can indicate, Your Honour, what it -- what the difficulty is. The Prosecution has been good enough to provide us with certain medical material. Our opinion is it doesn't suffice, but it leaves open the question. Rather than trouble Your Honour with it, I've asked for further particulars about it. And that's where the matter now stands. We don't require -- I'm sorry, I've used the term "writing," perhaps as shorthand, Your Honour, and I agree it's a habit of mine that will have to be cured. But Your Honour will be aware that there are some important interests at stake in having the witnesses present about which you may not require a speech from me right now. But it's important for Mr. Halilovic to have the witnesses present in court. These witnesses are capable of being controversial. I don't say that they are. But they may well be. So there is a genuine issue for decision. But I've indicated what our position is, and it may be that on Thursday we advise the Court that there is no issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that this is also a issue for the parties to discuss after this sitting. Yes. I think there are three Prosecution applications or submissions on my list, but most of them are concerning with the witnesses or exhibits. Could we deal with them on Thursday? Because it will go to the specifics of the particular witness. Is this agreeable?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And as for the 92 bis motions and expert reports, I prefer to defer the 92 bis motion at a later stage. The other motions are currently under the consideration by this Trial Chamber and will be ruled on in due course. But this morning we received another two new motions from the Defence team, and I wonder whether we could do it on Thursday morning or not. Yes. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, the Defence is certainly content for that to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Prosecution the title of those two new motions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, because we filed -- we thought we -- well, we filed, we believed, some -- some motions on Thursday. We just would ask to clarify which ones Your Honour is referring to there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think one is dated on the 24th January 2005, today; that is a response to Prosecution's motion to add and to withdraw exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. That's the one I referred to at the commencement of today's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And the other is a further addendum to the Defence response to Prosecution's motion to add and withdraw witnesses. This is a confidential filing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. That -- that latter filing relates to -- is a confidential filing. Does Your Honour wish us to provide details of that after today's session to the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe after today's session. I don't think the Prosecution has been noticed on those two motions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we have one of the motions, which is a strike out of the pleadings of our 65 ter filing, but not the other one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That's last week's motion. Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: They are very diligent in filing the motions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There's -- this response, we have just got it just before we came to court, so we confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The next issue is about witnesses and protective measures. And today we are going to have just preliminary discussions of the witness list. And I have a question to address to the Prosecution, that is, how many live witnesses the Prosecution are going to call.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: We are going to be calling 37 witnesses, including our expert witness, Mr. Ridgway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And how long do you think your case will last?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the indication we'd given at the 65 ter and the last Status Conference was two and a half to three months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I think we'll discuss the witness list on Thursday, but now I would like to give my initial response. I believe that the list of the live witnesses could be further shortened. For instance, from the pre-trial brief filed by the parties, especially by the Defence, I understand that there's no disputes on certain matters. For instance, on the crimes happened in Grabovica and Uzdol. Am I right, Mr. Morrissey? You do not deny that that murder happened in those two places?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, you are both right and wrong, with respect. There is a dispute as to a number of the victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There's no dispute that certain people -- that people were killed in each place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And without specifying who at this point, there will be no dispute that certain people were murdered in those places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. How about the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How about the perpetrators, the offenders? Are there any disputes on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's -- there's a difficulty about that because the Prosecution, we say, has not disclosed who they are, so we are -- we are in some -- some doubt about that. And it comes back to something raised by Your Honour before as to why we were seeking to strike paragraphs at this late stage and engaging in controversies that Your Honour would normally expect to be dealt with long ago and not raised at a late stage to embarrass the Prosecution. There's a historical reason for it that I'll raise now. It's, without engaging in the controversy, but it will assist Your Honour perhaps in understanding why it's happened. Long ago in the middle -- in fact, early -- I think at the end of 2003 a motion for further particulars was moved by the Defence and was dismissed by the Trial Chamber at the time later on the basis that sufficient notice was given because of the pleadings, the indictment, the pre-trial brief, and the supporting material, that being the witnesses. At that time the supporting material was much, much bigger than what is now before the Court. So there is, I have to say -- clearly there remains controversy as to who were the perpetrators. However, there are some who plainly are perpetrators. It may be disputed between the parties as to how many and where from, and that, I take it, is clear on the face of the material and in particular on the face of the material disclosed to us by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I quite understand your position. So it means that there's no dispute between the parties that atrocities, which is murder, happened during the places but there is still some disputes concerning the number of the victims as well as who the perpetrators are?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As to Grabovica, that accurately statements the situation. As to Uzdol, the situation is further complicated because although there is evidence that -- well, perhaps the whole crime base at Uzdol does create a problem. I'm not sure what to -- what knowledge to presume that Your Honour has in entering into detail here. I'll become detailed swiftly if not checked, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm just reading from the brief trials you submitted to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Our pre-trial brief, Your Honour, was submitted long ago and in relation to a case that has been changed quite significantly. So that whilst we have not sought at this point at all to change that pre-trial brief, Your Honour is now and we are now facing a different -- a case that is of a different colour, although it's still a 7(3) case. And there have been significant changes in recent times in response to which we have moved motions. And the matters raised by Your Honour, frankly we understand entirely. But we are, we think, facing a moving target, about which we have said much in our motions. And it's for that reason that I'm answering Your Honour in the equivocal way that I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I have some difficulty to appreciate your points at this moment. I think it's quite clear in the indictment. The -- your client is only charged with murder, and according to the Rule 7(3), that is, commander's responsibility. We also have such kind of saying in our jurisdiction, and it's kind of flying dishes, you know, in the shooting games, you know, we have the flying object and the fixed object, you know. But here from the indictment we see that the object is fixed already. That is the 7(3), murder. It's quite clear. But that's maybe just because I'm not quite familiar with this case. I did not read all the materials on this case at this moment, so I make these comments. But maybe later on I will learn more on it. But in this aspect, I still believe that, you know, there's some -- still some room for improvement to shorten the witness list or to shorten the direct examinations on certain witnesses. For instance, the -- you may sit down, please. The -- the video footages, you know, I believe that the Prosecution could use them in their opening statement and introduce them through the 92 bis if they do not go indirectly to the actual conduct of the accused. They only described the murder happened. This is, you know, just a suggestion, you know. I would hear the response from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll respond to that. There's something my learned friend, Mr. Morrissey said when he prefaced his remarks in response to Your Honour's question. And that was as to the identity of the perpetrators. Mr. Morrissey said that the Prosecution has not disclosed to the Defence who the perpetrators are. Now, the Prosecution takes very strong exception to that statement being made in this Pre-Trial Conference because it strikes -- it is an allegation that we are not complying with our disclosure obligations and that we are somehow withholding information from the Defence as to the identity of the perpetrators, whoever they may be. The Prosecution states very clearly on the record that we have provided all known material relating to the identity of the perpetrators to the Defence and we simply cannot take that matter any further. If he has any information that suggests other people are perpetrators, we ask him publicly to please provide it to us and we will look into it. Other than that, there's nothing more we can give them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have already noticed that point. But the Prosecution did not answer my question put to them. Are there any rooms for improvement by shortening the length of the testimony of the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour may not -- as Your Honour is not as familiar as the case -- with the case for the obvious -- obvious reasons you've just come into it. We've taken, I think, 69 witnesses from the original filed list, and we did that just before the break in late December. We take Your Honour's point. Of course there is always room for improvement. We will endeavour to cut the list further. We are also looking at the issue of the use of 89 -- Rule 89(F) and calling witnesses under 89(F), which should, if we can do it, reduce the proceedings further. In relation to the video, we certainly do intend to show the overhead videos of the crime scenes at Uzdol and Grabovica and if possible during the opening statement. We do not anticipate any objection from the Defence to us laying the groundwork there. If Your Honour is referring to the BBC journalist, Ms. Adie's video, that of course depends upon agreement with the Defence as to whether they wish to cross-examine the witnesses. A lot of the points Your Honours -- Your Honour has raised very much -- are very much up in the air at the moment. It depends upon cooperation with the Defence as to how we can limit the -- the case. We are anxious to limit it and to confine it to the issues of the accused's responsibility under Article 7(3). We will be meeting -- we have met with Mr. Morrissey. We will attempt to do it again, and -- on Thursday morning I hope we will be in a position to report back to Your Honour. Does that answer Your Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But my question is posing to you, that is, for instance, as for the first witness, can you let the Defence do the cross-examination only if they need a cross-examination, without any direct examination on your part?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The -- probably not with the first couple of witnesses. They are live crime -- live crime-scene witnesses. The Prosecution, as Your Honour appreciates, would wish to mix some live crime-scene witnesses who can identify the direct perpetrators, which goes to the identity of those who committed them -- committed the crimes and whether or not they were under the accused's effective control. We wish to mix those with some witnesses who can give their evidence under 89(F) or possibly, according to the rulings, in relation to the ambit of 7(3) responsibility, under 92 bis. So with the first couple, probably not. But as we move into the trial, we certainly want to try and limit the live testimony, if we can, according to Your Honour's directions. But again that, depends very much upon the Defence and how much they will agree to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. And generally speaking, the Bench would like to hear one witness for one day, including cross-examination. Since there are 37 witnesses -- live witnesses in this case, I wonder if eight weeks - that is, two months - will be possible for the Prosecution to finish her case.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, that sounds like a sensible estimate, but we would like to say there would be some witnesses who probably will not take a morning session and, as opposed to others, who might even take a couple of days. So I don't know if that would feature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Generally speaking, is it feasible to finish your case in eight weeks?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will certainly endeavour to finish it by eight weeks. And I think that's a reasonable estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I understand there's no protective measures or delayed disclosure of identity of the witness as being requested during the pre-trial phase of this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. We have not filed any -- any protective measures for any of the witnesses, Your Honours, simply because we've been asking the witnesses if they can justify such protective measures being sought from -- from the Chamber. But as we go along and as we proof them, if there are some concerns that they display, we will certainly be filing such motions at the time. But at this time, we haven't filed any because, as I said, we have not been entirely satisfied ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I just want to bear in mind that as a rule all the trial should be conducted in the open session unless there's some extraordinary reasons justifying your request. As a practice -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I didn't mean to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But prior to another topic. I would simply ask to put on record that we ask to be given a sufficient opportunity to respond to any such motion, by which I mean not being told on the morning that such a motion is to be moved, because we would want to be heard about it. And so bearing in mind what Your Honour has just said, I need add no more than to say we would want to be heard on any such motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. As for the totally closed session as well as the voice distortion, I believe that the Prosecution or the party calling the witness should inform the Chamber one day before the testimony. As for the other protective measures, we will do it on the morning or a few minutes before the witness enters into the room. Is that agreeable?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I see everybody is nodding. As a practice in other trials, I would like to make an oral order to request the Prosecutor to file all the witness statements tomorrow so that we could deal with each witness in the second phase of the Pre-Trial Conference, Thursday. Is that agreeable to the parties?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you going to file in the electronic form or in the written form?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's -- it is the e-court. I suppose you'd probably want them in electronic form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If you have already prepared the written forms, you know, we'll be very glad to receive them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: If Your Honour would be glad to have the written ones, we'll, of course, provide them in written form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any objections, Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, there isn't. But we just note that there are some statements that would appear to be outstanding that haven't been provided to anyone as yet. These are the statements from witnesses Miletic, Husic, H-u-s-i-c, and Mujezinovic, M-u-j-e-z-i-n-o-v-i-c. With respect to those three, each of those refers in material provided to other statements which they've provided. Those have not been in fact provided so that we ask that they be provided both to us and in the way that Your Honour has just requested they be provided to the Court. Because at the moment what we have is a witness referring to -- this is the second time I have spoken and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you alleging that the Prosecution did not finish their obligation to disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's an allegation to that effect in motions already, which you don't need to have rehearsed now, unless you ask me and give me permission to do. So I simply mention it now because Your Honour has asked that statements be provided. And we just point out that to our analysis - and we don't have the knowledge the Prosecutor has as yet - there seem to be three missing, and we'd be very grateful for them and we think it's an issue that will need to be addressed to comply with what Your Honour has just raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any signed papers on the side of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have this morning got the Mujezinovic statement that we are going to provide to the Defence. But the other two, Your Honour, which is the Miletic and the Husic, we have disclosed them, and the receipt numbers are 38 and 48. And the -- and also the Husic statement has been disclosed, and the receipts are 33, 34, 35, 48, and 74. So while all the -- there's only one statement that Defence counsel alludes to which we are going to now disclose, the Mujezinovic statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. But you did not tell me the reason for such late disclosure yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, this has -- this is an issue which I would actually have liked to have raised with the Chamber at some other time, but I can raise it now. There are a lot of motions relating to disclosure and late disclosure. I will just talk about this particular one statement of this one witness. And the reason is, is simply it's been an oversight. We had not got it before. It's only when the Defence counsel says that there should be another one, we looked through our documents again and we found this one statement. But all the others had been disclosed. There's no other way to put it, Your Honours. It's an oversight. And for which, of course, we do sincerely apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I hope Mr. Morrissey will accept the apology from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: When an assurance like that is given in court, of course we accept it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But at the same time I have to warn the Prosecution that you have to pay due diligence to your work in this aspect, especially when we're going on to trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm remind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, may I have the indulgence to say one more thing? I am reminded that the Prosecutor have been for some time now under a requirement that they seek leave to provide such material. That's an order that was imposed upon them on the 15th of -- of -- sorry, 7th of May of last year, and it's a reason why Your Honour will see -- well, I'm about to launch into a submission. I won't. I'm sorry. I simply mention what I mentioned and that will suffice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for reminding me of this issue, and I'll look into it, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: With your leave, I would like to bring up this matter of this issue that Defence counsel has raised, about the 7th of May order given by the Trial Chamber that we have to seek leave of the Chamber for anything we disclose after December -- the 15th December 2003. And this also includes, Your Honour, disclosure under Rule 68. Now, this has become a very onerous burden on the Prosecution because inevitably we have new material which has come in and, as we all know, that our document collections are huge. Your Honour, the whole purpose of disclosure is for the benefit of the Defence, and we would like to hand it over as quickly as we get it. And there will be times when things have been overlooked. It's inevitable. It happens in all the other trials here. And this has been one of the cause of the prolific motions the Defence counsel have been filing and it all relates to disclosure and it is all to do with this one decision that we have. Your Honour, the other day we disclosed eight - I believe it was eight, I'll be corrected by Defence counsel if it was seven - Rule 68 documents. Now, the decision also states that Defence counsel may waive this requirement and receive this disclosure. But every time I've sought the indulgence of the Defence to waive it and simply hand over at least the Rule 68 documents, they have not agreed to waive it. Now, it's clear that all disclosure is for the benefit of the Defence. And I am somewhat perplexed that the Defence do not wish to receive this material as quickly as possible. And they want -- they do sit on their rights under this decision. I think I would -- one of the -- the other issues, Your Honour, I would now ask -- perhaps since there are going to be -- we're going to have another conference on Thursday, perhaps Your Honours would look into this matter, because I would now orally like you to vacate this particular order. And in that event, it become easier -- easier management. And in respect of, let's say, Celo statements, there were four statements which we had not disclosed. Celo is Ramiz Delalic. He's one of the -- one of our witnesses which we asked to be added to the list subsequent, in our new witness list. And these four statements had already been put into the EDS, electronic suite. But at that time, Ramiz Delalic was not our witness, so we had not disclosed his previous statements. But we -- we have the ABiH collections which came into this Office after the particular date of 15th December. Therefore, those -- the moment we put Mr. Delalic on the witness list, we ran the searches. We found these four additional statements. We immediately informed the Defence that we have these additional statements. And I said, "Can I just disclose them to you and would you waive the requirement that we have to do it by way of motion?" And the response has always been, "No, we have to do it by way of motion." The Prosecution has been courteous in providing the material before on an informal basis and then doing the motion late -- later on. I am not aware as to any other Trial Chamber who has issued such an order at this Tribunal. This is an unprecedented order against the Prosecution. And I do not think that it assists the Defence either. Disclosure is for their benefit, and we are finding these documents. And I think the Defence would be prejudiced if they would not want to get the disclosure as quickly as possible. So once again, I would ask this Trial Chamber to vacate this order and in the event there's any disclosure that the Defence feels particularly prejudiced by, they may raise that particular issue and we will respond accordingly to anything which the Defence feel that has been -- has somehow prejudiced their case or the conduct of their trial. And then we would -- rather than every single disclosure we have to seek the -- the leave of the Trial Chamber, we disclose to the Defence, "this is my recommendation." And if they feel there is anything that prejudices them, they may then ask by motion for any explanation as to -- and then the Court can rule upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please be very concise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I will be. May I direct Your Honour to the Defence response to the 20th of January of this year to a Prosecution motion to add Rule 66(A) material relating to the witness Ramiz Delalic, also known as Celo. Your Honour will have noticed that five minutes ago I commenced what I was about to launch into as a submission and did not do so, and I hear Your Honour's requirement to be concise. The reason why the Prosecution has been placed in the position it has been and the reason why it's compelled to disclose in the way it has is because the history of the disclosure practices of the Prosecution in this case have been appalling. I rely on what's been filed and don't seek to make a speech about it here. But when Your Honour reviews that sorry history, you will see that despite orders of the Court, suggestions by the judicial representative at Rule 65 ter conferences, undertakings by the Prosecution that disclosure has finally finished, it never did. And disclosure has continued unabated in ways unexpected and in ways which have fundamentally changed the case, resulting in a series of Prosecution motions in December of this year, followed by a series of motions by us in January. And if our submissions have any merit, they are in writing before the Court, before the Chamber, and I won't seek to re-canvass them here. But it's into that context that Your Honour's Chamber now comes, and it's into that context that of rules and restrictions being placed upon the Prosecution as far as their discovery practice go that we now stand, and it's for that reason that we've sought the protection of the Chamber in the way that we have from continued disclosure. That's what this flurry of motions is about: Protection. And that's all I have to say about it in line with Your Honour's suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. There must be a reason for the Pre-Trial Chamber to render an order in this respect. And I promise you, both parties, I'll look into this matter and to see whether there's something I can do to facilitate the proceedings of this case. Thank you. And the last matter on our agenda is the agreed facts. During the last Status Conference, the Pre-Trial Judge requested both parties to meet and to try to come to some agreed facts. I would like to know from the parties about the results. Mr. Morrissey, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said both yes and no earlier today, and I now say it again. If we are having what I describe as constructive discussions, the Defence has provided a list of -- of potential agreed facts. The Prosecution has not had time to respond to those, and it's not the Prosecution's fault, because I provided those very lately to them, so that they're entitled some time about that to consider those. The Prosecution has provided some suggestions to us. We bear in mind all of our undertakings in the past. We don't here have a list of agreed facts to give to the Chamber. We are meeting -- we met today. We will meet again. We have not forgotten the matter. But we do not have a satisfactory answer for you on it immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could I turn to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That is the correct position, Your Honour. We have met but -- but very briefly. I have received a document this morning proposing some agreed facts by the Defence. And as Defence counsel indicated, he has some agreed facts from us. And we will now endeavour -- I think we've been all very busy trying to prepare for this case, but I think that's a very important aspect, given the guidance -- Your Honour's guidance this morning about the case and perhaps we can now sit down before Thursday and see if we can come up with some more arrangement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the purpose for the parties to meet is to identify some common ground in ending some disputes, so that the Trial Chamber will be in a more clear position to hear the case so that we know such matters are still in the dispute but certain matters has already, you know, exist some agreements. For instance, the position of the accused that the Pre-Trial Judge mentioned last time and the whereabouts of the accused during that critical period. I just, you know -- you know, give some examples. But if there's no agreement, I also hope that the parties will submit us with something identified those differences. I hope that before the next Pre-Trial Conference, that is, on Thursday, we could receive a report from the parties on those issues. Is that agreeable to the parties? It seems to me that everybody is nodding.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's -- it certainly is to the agreement of the Defence. I'm just not familiar with -- with the structure of such a report. And in the new e-world in which we live, would Your Honour give some guidance as to whether we are allowed to use paper in that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's a practice before some other Chambers --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- that, you know, one party will propose some items both in agreement or in disagreement, you know. And they identify those areas and tell us what is still in dispute and what is not in dispute. And some of these reports are based on the indictment. For instance, the certain paragraph we have problems, you know. We have disputes on that paragraph. But on certain paragraphs we have no disputes at all. For instance, the background information about the accused. There's no disputes -- generally speaking, no disputes. At least we could know where we are in this case. We could nail down the crucial points in this case, which will be facilitating the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We'll cooperate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I will not force anybody to any agreement that you don't like to make with the other party. I have to say that very clear. You may sit down, please. And at this stage, are there any other matters the parties would like to mention? From the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Not at this -- at this stage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. From the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There's one unusual matter that I would like to raise now, and it's fortunate that it's -- that perhaps it could be thought about. I haven't raised it with the Prosecution either as of yet, save in passing. I think it's been mentioned in casual conversation. It's the position of the accused man in the courtroom. Now, the normal position is that Mr. Halilovic would be seated where he is, some distance away from the Defence team. Now, we would seek the indulgence that he be permitted to sit with us. It's an unusual submission, but there are reasons for it. The first and main reason is that this being a command responsibility case and at least lead counsel on the Defence side not being a military person although seized of the relevant facts and doctrines in the case, I hope, would benefit greatly in the efficient running of the trial by the presence near at hand of Mr. Halilovic. He was on any view of it a person -- well, he was a general. He's able to comment directly upon the doctrines and the applicability of those doctrines as the evidence arises in court. True it is he can tell us - and he has already done so on many indication occasions - the meaning of particular doctrines and documents, but in court evidence is going to come out viva voce and might come out in a variety of ways. It would greatly assist the Defence if he were able to do that. In support of this, I put this: That's he's been on provisional release for a long time with no blemishes, as I understand the matter. He remained on provisional release. He returned to the court, to the Tribunal as he was required to do. And, in short, he can be regarded as a person in responsibility in respect of whose courtroom conduct you need have no fear. And therefore, you could expect that he would conduct himself well. We are not aware of - although, we could never be aware of ourselves, I admit - any security objection to this. There may be protocols that we don't know about, and they're matters that would have to be raised by others and not by us. But we would accommodate any seating arrangements and we would accommodate security. If they felt there needed to be any nearby, we would accommodate that. It's a matter of significance to the Defence to have that done. Of course, there is the additional matter, shared with all accused, it has to be said, of the stigmatisation and so on that goes with where he's positioned. But, of course, we bear in mind that the Bench will not be swayed by that matter. Nevertheless, it is a humiliating matter for any accused. If it can be avoided, if as a matter of proportion it can be avoided, then there's no reason why it shouldn't be. If there's no good reason, in short, for Mr. Halilovic to be where he is now, we invite him and hope that the Court would -- would permit us to invite him to come and sit amongst us and assist us in presenting his case as swiftly and efficiently has can humanly be. Therefore, I make that application on the spot here in court and ask that it be considered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any response from the Prosecution side?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an unusual request that the accused sit at a bar table. Can we please respond and take the position, as my learned friend indicated, there are security issues, and this is a larger policy issue. And if I can take advice on the matter and respond on Thursday, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Morrissey, I believe that seating in this courtroom has been arranged by the Registrar. Where the Judges sit, the Defence counsel sits, and the Prosecution sits are all arranged beforehand, including your client, the accused. So certainly I will convey your suggestions to the attention of the Registrar to see whether there's any possibility for some changes in that seating. I believe this is what I can do at this stage. As you know, the Registrar is a separate section of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could -- could I indicate that we ask no more than that. Mr. Halilovic knows well that it may cause inconvenience and appreciates the risk that it's possible that this request cannot be accommodated and he and we will abide the decision of the Court and he -- well, we indicate our appreciation for the temperate stance taken by the Prosecutor, and we are appreciative too that Your Honour will consider the matter, as you've indicated, and we say no more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. So if there's nothing else the parties would like to raise, the hearing is adjourned. And we'll continue on Thursday morning.
